Chinese: Kung Fu/Wushu (umbrella term for many styles — Wing Chun, Shaolin, Tai Chi), Tai Chi (meditative, slow movements, internal energy). Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ): developed by the Gracie family from Japanese judo/jujutsu — focuses on ground fighting and submissions. Demonstrated that a smaller person can defeat a larger one using leverage and technique. Boxing: 'the sweet science' — 8 weight classes from strawweight (47.6 kg) to heavyweight (90+ kg). Muhammad Ali (1942-2016): widely considered the greatest — 56-5 record, 'float like a butterfly, sting like a bee.' MMA (Mixed Martial Arts): UFC (founded 1993) combines striking and grappling disciplines.

Electronic music evolved from early synthesizers and tape manipulation. Key developments: Moog synthesizer (Robert Moog, 1964 — enabled affordable electronic music), Kraftwerk (German pioneers of electronic music, 1970s — influenced virtually all electronic music since), Roland TR-808 drum machine (1980, its bass drum sound is in thousands of songs — distinctive boom), Roland TB-303 bassline synthesizer (1981 — accidental discovery of the acid house sound). Genres: Disco (1970s New York — 4/4 kick drum, orchestral, gay club scene), House (Chicago, early 1980s — Frankie Knuckles at The Warehouse), Techno (Detroit, mid-1980s — Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson — 'The Belleville Three'), Trance (Germany, early 1990s — emotional, melodic), Drum and Bass/Jungle (UK, 1990s — fast breakbeats ~174 BPM), Dubstep (South London, early 2000s — Skream, Benga, Digital Mystikz — evolved into EDM 'brostep' via Skrillex). Deadmau5, Daft Punk, Avicii, Calvin Harris, David Guetta defined mainstream EDM.

The Beatles (John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, Ringo Starr) are the best-selling music artists in history — 600 million+ records sold. From Liverpool, formed 1960. Manager Brian Epstein, producer George Martin ('Fifth Beatle'). US arrival Feb 9, 1964 (Ed Sullivan Show — 73 million viewers, 45% of US population) launched Beatlemania and the British Invasion. Evolution: early Merseybeat pop ('Please Please Me,' 'She Loves You') → sophisticated rock ('Rubber Soul,' 1965) → psychedelia ('Revolver,' 1966; 'Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band,' 1967 — first concept album?) → 'White Album' (1968) → 'Abbey Road' (1969) → Let It Be (1970, breakup). Lennon-McCartney: greatest songwriting partnership in pop history. Lennon assassinated Dec 8, 1980 in New York. McCartney still tours at 80+. The Rolling Stones: formed 1962, 'World's Greatest Rock and Roll Band,' still touring — Mick Jagger, Keith Richards.

Globalization: the increasing interconnection of the world's economies, cultures, and populations through trade, communication, and migration. The WTO (World Trade Organization, founded 1995, 164 members): sets global trade rules and resolves disputes. Free trade agreements (FTAs): reduce tariffs and barriers between member countries — NAFTA/USMCA (USA/Canada/Mexico), EU single market, TPP/CPTPP. Comparative advantage (Ricardo, 1817): countries benefit from specializing in what they produce most efficiently and trading — even if one country is better at everything. Global supply chains: Apple designs in California, sources components from 43 countries, manufactures in China, sells globally. COVID-19 revealed supply chain vulnerabilities — computer chip shortage shut down car production. Deglobalization trends: geopolitical tensions, reshoring ('friend-shoring'), and supply chain diversification. China's Belt and Road Initiative: infrastructure lending and development across 150+ countries — criticized as 'debt trap diplomacy.'

World population: 8 billion reached November 15, 2022. Growth: from 1 billion (1804) → 2B (1927) → 3B (1960) → 4B (1974) → 5B (1987) → 6B (1999) → 7B (2011) → 8B (2022). Projected ~10 billion by 2050-2100 then stabilization/decline. Demographic transition: as countries develop, birth rates fall after death rates — high birth/death → high birth/low death (population boom) → low birth/low death (stable). Fertility rate of 2.1 children per woman maintains stable population. Most of Europe, East Asia, and Latin America are below replacement fertility. Japan, South Korea, Italy, Germany are shrinking. Africa and parts of South Asia still growing. Aging: by 2050, 2 billion people will be over 65 (vs 700 million today). Migration: ~281 million international migrants worldwide (3.6% of world population). Climate change projected to drive 200 million+ climate refugees by 2050.

Global inequality: the world's 2,668 billionaires have as much wealth as the bottom 60% of humanity combined (Oxfam). Gini coefficient: measures income inequality (0 = perfect equality, 1 = one person has everything). Most equal: Nordic countries (Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland — Gini ~0.25-0.28). Most unequal: South Africa (0.63), Brazil, Colombia, Namibia, Zambia. US Gini: ~0.41 (high for a wealthy nation). Extreme poverty: World Bank defines as living under $2.15/day (2022 dollars) — dropped from 36% of world population (1990) to ~9% (2022) — massive progress. About 700 million people still live in extreme poverty. Human Rights: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UN, 1948, Eleanor Roosevelt was instrumental): 30 articles establishing civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights. The UN Human Rights Council monitors violations. NGOs: Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch document violations globally.

Mass media evolution: printing press (Gutenberg, ~1440) → newspapers (17th century) → radio (1920s) → television (1950s) → internet (1990s) → social media (2000s) → algorithms (2010s+). News media: broadsheets (NYT, Washington Post, Guardian, Le Monde), tabloids, broadcast news (BBC, CNN, Fox News), public radio (NPR, BBC Radio). Misinformation/disinformation: false information spreading faster than corrections on social media — MIT study (2018): false news spread 6× faster than true news on Twitter. Algorithms: optimize for engagement (outrage, fear, and tribalism drive more clicks) — reinforcing filter bubbles and polarization. 'Deep fakes': AI-generated fake videos of real people — increasingly convincing and dangerous. Media literacy: critical skills to evaluate source credibility, identify bias, and check information across multiple sources. Journalistic ethics: independence, accuracy, fairness, accountability, minimizing harm. Newspapers' business model is in crisis (ad revenue → Google/Facebook); many local papers have closed.

There are ~7,100 languages spoken worldwide — half may be extinct by 2100. Most spoken by native speakers: Mandarin Chinese (~920 million), Spanish (~475 million), English (~370 million), Hindi (~340 million), Arabic (~315 million), Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Japanese, Yue Chinese (Cantonese). Most spoken including second-language speakers: English (1.5 billion total). Languages die at ~2 per week. The Linguistic Society of America (1924) and UNESCO work on language documentation. Language families: Indo-European (English, Spanish, Hindi, Russian, Persian — descended from a common ancestor ~6,000 years ago), Sino-Tibetan (Mandarin, Tibetan, Burmese), Afro-Asiatic (Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic), Niger-Congo (Swahili, Yoruba, Zulu — 1,500+ languages), Austronesian (Malay, Tagalog, Hawaiian, Māori). Sign languages are full natural languages — ASL (American Sign Language) has its own grammar different from English.

English has borrowed extensively from Latin and Ancient Greek — understanding roots unlocks thousands of words. Latin roots: aqua (water: aquatic, aquarium), bene (good: benefit, benevolent), bio (life: biology, biography), cent (hundred: century, percent), dict (say: dictate, dictionary, predict), duc/duce (lead: conduct, deduce, education), fac/fact (make/do: factory, manufacture, artifact), juris (law: jury, justice, jurisdiction), locus (place: location, local), mal (bad: malfunction, malevolent), man/manu (hand: manual, manufacture), mort (death: mortal, immortal), port (carry: transport, portable, export), scrib/script (write: describe, manuscript, inscription), spec/spect (look: spectacle, inspect), terra (earth: territory, terrain), vid/vis (see: video, visible, vision), vit/viv (live: vital, vivid). Greek roots: chrono (time), demos (people), geo (earth), logos (word/study), micro/macro, mono/poly, ology (study of), phone (sound), photo (light), tele (far), thermo (heat).

Money's three functions: medium of exchange (avoids barter), store of value (save purchasing power), and unit of account (measure value). Types: commodity money (gold, silver — intrinsic value), representative money (backed by a commodity), fiat money (value by government decree — all modern currencies). The US dollar: world's reserve currency since Bretton Woods Agreement (1944) — most global trade is priced in dollars. Central banks: set interest rates (higher rates → more expensive to borrow → less spending/investment → reduces inflation; lower rates → opposite). The Federal Reserve (US): 'dual mandate' — stable prices AND maximum employment. ECB (Europe). Inflation: too much money chasing too few goods. Hyperinflation: Zimbabwe (2008 — 79.6 billion percent monthly inflation rate, prices doubling every 24 hours), Weimar Germany (1923), Venezuela (2018+). Deflation: falling prices sound good but cause economic death spirals (consumers wait to buy, businesses can't invest). Central banks target ~2% inflation as ideal.

Silicon Valley (San Francisco Bay Area) has been the world's innovation hub since the semiconductor industry emerged in the 1950s-60s (Fairchild Semiconductor, Intel). Why there: Stanford and Berkeley universities, venture capital ecosystem, risk-accepting culture, dense network of founders and talent. Venture capital (VC): investors provide capital to early-stage companies in exchange for equity — accepting high risk for potential outsized returns. Stages: pre-seed/angel → seed → Series A → B → C → D... IPO (Initial Public Offering): first sale of shares to the public on a stock exchange. Unicorn: private startup valued at $1 billion+ (coined by Aileen Lee, 2013). Decacorn: $10B+. Hectocorn: $100B+. Key VC firms: Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Benchmark, Accel, Kleiner Perkins. The Lean Startup (Eric Ries): build-measure-learn feedback loop, minimum viable product (MVP). Most startups fail: ~90% within 10 years. 'Fail fast' philosophy.

Space exploration milestones: Sputnik (USSR, Oct 4, 1957 — first satellite), Laika (first animal in space, 1957), Yuri Gagarin (first human in space, April 12, 1961, 108 minutes), John Glenn (first American to orbit Earth, 1962), Apollo 11 Moon landing (July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin — 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'), Apollo 13 (1970, 'Houston we have a problem,' remarkable rescue mission). Space Shuttle program (1981-2011): 135 missions, 2 disasters (Challenger 1986, Columbia 2003). ISS (International Space Station): continuously inhabited since November 2000, 16-nation collaboration. New space race: SpaceX (reusable rockets, Starship), Blue Origin (Jeff Bezos, New Shepard and New Glenn), NASA Artemis program (return humans to Moon, aim for 2025-2026), Chinese space program (Tiangong space station, lunar ambitions), commercial lunar economy. Voyager 1 (launched 1977): now 24+ billion km from Earth — the farthest human-made object.

Photography fundamentals — the 'exposure triangle': Aperture (f-stop): the opening in the lens. Wider aperture (smaller f-number: f/1.4, f/2) = more light, shallower depth of field (blurry background — 'bokeh'). Narrower aperture (f/11, f/16) = less light, more of the scene in focus. Shutter speed: duration the sensor is exposed. Faster (1/1000s): freezes motion. Slower (1/30s, 1s+): blurs motion, requires tripod. ISO: sensor sensitivity. Lower ISO (100, 200): less light absorbed, cleaner image. Higher ISO (3200, 6400+): more sensitive but adds 'noise' (grain). Composition rules (guidelines, not laws): Rule of thirds (divide frame into 3×3 grid, place subjects at intersections), leading lines (guide viewer's eye), framing (use foreground elements), symmetry, negative space, and 'if in doubt, zoom out.' RAW vs JPEG: RAW files contain all sensor data (much larger, requires editing software but far more flexibility) vs JPEG (compressed, ready to share).

Architecture history: Ancient: Pyramids of Giza (~2560 BC), Parthenon (Athens, 447 BC), Roman Colosseum (80 AD), Pantheon (125 AD — unreinforced concrete dome still standing). Medieval: Gothic cathedrals — flying buttresses transferred weight outward enabling tall thin walls with huge stained glass windows (Notre-Dame de Paris, Chartres, Cologne Cathedral). Renaissance: symmetry, proportion, classical references (Brunelleschi's Florence Cathedral dome — the first large dome since Antiquity). Baroque: dramatic, ornate, theatrical (St. Peter's Basilica, Versailles). Modernism (20th century): 'form follows function' (Louis Sullivan), glass and steel, rejection of ornamentation — Bauhaus school (Gropius), Le Corbusier (brutalism), Mies van der Rohe (minimalism). Frank Lloyd Wright: organic architecture, Fallingwater (cantilevered over a waterfall), Guggenheim Museum. Tallest buildings: Burj Khalifa, Dubai (828m, 2010); Merdeka 118, Malaysia (679m, 2023); Shanghai Tower (632m).

Plastic pollution: ~400 million tonnes of plastic produced annually; ~14 million tonnes enter the ocean per year. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch: a gyre of marine debris twice the size of Texas (~1.6 million km²), mostly microplastics (not a solid island — dispersed particles). Microplastics (<5mm): breakdown of larger plastics; also from synthetic clothing washing (microfibers), tire wear, and industrial processes. Found in: Arctic snow, deep ocean trenches (Mariana Trench), Arctic sea ice, human blood (2022 study), breast milk, placentas, and the air. Health effects: under active research. Only ~9% of all plastic ever produced has been recycled; 12% was incinerated; 79% is in landfills or the environment. Solutions: reduce single-use plastics, improve waste management in developing countries (most ocean plastic comes from Asia — especially rivers), extended producer responsibility, chemical recycling. Plastic takes 450+ years to decompose.

Human evolution: Hominins (bipedal apes) diverged from chimpanzees ~6-7 million years ago. Key ancestors: Australopithecus (3.9-2.9 Ma, Africa — Lucy skeleton discovered 1974, 3.2 million years old), Homo habilis ('handy man,' ~2.4-1.4 Ma — first stone tools), Homo erectus (1.9 Ma-140,000 years ago — first hominin to leave Africa, mastered fire), Homo heidelbergensis, Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthals, 400,000-40,000 years ago — Europe and Asia, large brains, used tools, buried dead, made art; Homo sapiens interbred with them — non-Africans are ~2% Neanderthal). Homo sapiens: anatomically modern humans evolved in Africa ~300,000 years ago. Out of Africa migration: ~60,000-70,000 years ago — expanded across the world, reaching Australia ~65,000 years ago, Americas ~15,000+ years ago. The 'Great Leap Forward' ~50,000 years ago: sudden behavioral modernity — complex art, music, ritual, and symbolic thinking (cave art in Chauvet Cave, 36,000 years old).

AI history: Alan Turing (1912-1954): broke the Enigma code in WWII, proposed the 'Turing Test' (1950 — if a machine's conversation is indistinguishable from a human's, it can be considered 'intelligent'), invented theoretical foundations of computing. 'The Imitation Game' (2014 film). Dartmouth Conference (1956): John McCarthy coined 'artificial intelligence.' Early AI: symbolic AI ('good old-fashioned AI') — explicit rules and logic. AI winters (1974-80, 1987-93): hype exceeded progress, funding dried up. Expert systems (1980s): knowledge bases. Machine learning (1980s-90s): algorithms learned from data. Deep Blue (IBM, 1997): defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov — milestone in narrow AI. ImageNet and deep learning breakthrough (2012, AlexNet): convolutional neural networks dramatically outperformed other methods in image recognition — sparked the modern deep learning era. AlphaGo (DeepMind, 2016): defeated Lee Sedol 4-1 at Go (far harder than chess — 10^170 possible positions). GPT-3 (OpenAI, 2020) and ChatGPT (2022): large language models surprised the world with general conversational ability.

Legal systems worldwide: Common law (UK, USA, Canada, Australia): judge-made case law ('precedent') shapes the law — courts are bound by past decisions (stare decisis). Civil law (France, Germany, Japan, most of Europe and Latin America): comprehensive legal codes, less emphasis on precedent. Sharia law: Islamic law from Quran and Hadith — used in varying degrees in Muslim-majority countries (Saudi Arabia, Iran: strictly; others: partially or in family law only). Constitutional law: a constitution is the supreme law — all other laws must comply. US Bill of Rights (First 10 Amendments): freedom of speech/religion/press, right to bear arms, protection from unreasonable searches, right to jury trial, protection against self-incrimination, due process, right to an attorney. International law: treaties (binding agreements between states), customary international law, ICC (International Criminal Court — prosecutes war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide). Habeas corpus: the right not to be imprisoned without legal justification — a cornerstone of civil liberty.

The ancient Olympics began in 776 BC at Olympia, Greece — held every 4 years (Olympiad) in honor of Zeus. Athletes competed nude, only Greek men allowed (though Spartan women competed in a separate festival). Events: foot races (stadion = ~192m — origin of 'stadium'), wrestling, discus, javelin, chariot racing. Theodosius I abolished them in 393 AD as pagan. Pierre de Coubertin (French educator) revived the Olympics — first modern games in Athens, 1896: 14 nations, 241 athletes, 43 events. Now: 200+ nations, 10,000+ athletes, 300+ events, alternating Summer (every 4 years) and Winter Games (also every 4 years, offset by 2). 2024 Summer: Paris. The Paralympic Games (for athletes with physical disabilities) was formalized in 1960, now held alongside every Olympics. World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) tests athletes. Most decorated Olympian: Michael Phelps (28 medals). Most gold: Michael Phelps (23). Most Olympic team medals: USA (Summer), Norway (Winter).

Renewable energy sources: Solar photovoltaic (PV): silicon cells convert sunlight directly to electricity. Cost has fallen 90% since 2010 — now the cheapest electricity in history in most places. Global solar capacity: 1+ terawatt. Wind turbines: convert kinetic energy of wind. Offshore wind is more expensive to build but wind is stronger and more consistent. Denmark gets 55%+ of its electricity from wind. Hydroelectric: dams use falling water to generate electricity — largest source of renewable electricity (16% of global total). Three Gorges Dam (China): world's largest power station (22.5 GW). Geothermal: heat from Earth's interior — Iceland gets 66% of its energy from geothermal. Batteries/storage: key challenge — renewables are intermittent (sun doesn't always shine, wind doesn't always blow). Lithium-ion batteries (Tesla Megapack, utility-scale), pumped hydro, and green hydrogen are key storage solutions. Global clean energy investment exceeded $1 trillion for the first time in 2022. Coal use is declining; natural gas is the transition fuel. Nuclear debate continues — low carbon but expensive and slow to build.

Greatest scientists in history: Isaac Newton (1643-1727): laws of motion and universal gravitation, calculus (simultaneously with Leibniz), optics. 'If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.' Charles Darwin (1809-1882): theory of evolution by natural selection ('On the Origin of Species,' 1859) — the most important idea in biology. Marie Curie (1867-1934): discovered polonium and radium, first woman to win a Nobel Prize, only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911). She died from aplastic anemia caused by radiation exposure. Nikola Tesla (1856-1943): AC electrical system (vs Edison's DC), induction motor, Tesla coil. Albert Einstein (1879-1955): Special and General Relativity, photoelectric effect (Nobel 1921), E=mc². Richard Feynman (1918-1988): quantum electrodynamics (Nobel 1965), Feynman diagrams, brilliant teacher. Rosalind Franklin: X-ray crystallography crucial to discovering DNA structure (her contribution was underacknowledged — Watson, Crick, and Wilkins got the Nobel).

The human skeleton has 206 bones in adults (babies have ~270-300, many fuse). Functions: support, protection, movement, mineral storage (99% of body's calcium and phosphorus), and blood cell production (in bone marrow). Bone types: long (femur, humerus), short (wrist/ankle), flat (skull, ribs, sternum — protect organs), irregular (vertebrae), sesamoid (patella/kneecap). Bone tissue: compact (dense outer layer) and spongy/trabecular (porous inner network). Bones are living tissue — constantly remodeled by osteoblasts (build) and osteoclasts (break down). Peak bone density: age 25-30. Osteoporosis: bones become porous and brittle, especially post-menopausal women (estrogen protects bones). Most commonly broken bone: clavicle (collarbone). Strongest bone: femur (thighbone — can withstand force of 1,700-2,500 lbs before breaking).

The human body has ~600 named muscles making up ~40% of body weight. Three types: skeletal (voluntary, striated — moves bones), smooth (involuntary — lines organs, blood vessels, digestive tract), cardiac (heart — involuntary, striated, never fatigues). Skeletal muscle anatomy: muscle → fascicles → muscle fibers → myofibrils → sarcomeres (functional unit). Contraction: sliding filament theory — actin and myosin filaments slide past each other using ATP energy. Muscle fiber types: Type I (slow-twitch, fatigue-resistant, aerobic — endurance), Type IIa (fast-twitch, moderate endurance), Type IIx (fast-twitch, high force, fatigues quickly — sprinting, lifting). DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness): occurs 24-72 hours after exercise — caused by micro-tears and inflammation, not lactic acid. Largest muscle: gluteus maximus. Strongest: masseter (jaw). Smallest: stapedius (in ear, 1mm).

Digestion: mechanical (chewing, churning) and chemical (enzymes, acids) breakdown of food into absorbable nutrients. Journey: mouth (amylase begins starch digestion) → esophagus (peristalsis — 4-8 sec) → stomach (hydrochloric acid pH 1.5-3.5, pepsin digests protein, 2-4 hour transit) → small intestine (~6-7m, 3-5 hour transit — 90% of nutrient absorption via villi and microvilli that increase surface area to ~250 m² — the size of a tennis court) → large intestine (~1.5m, water absorption, fermentation by gut bacteria, 10-59 hour transit) → rectum → anus. Gut microbiome: ~38 trillion bacteria (more than human cells), 1,000+ species, 1-2 kg total weight. Functions: ferment fiber, produce vitamins (K2, B12, biotin), train immune system, influence mood (90% of serotonin produced in gut — the 'gut-brain axis'). Liver produces bile (stored in gallbladder) to emulsify fats.

The respiratory system exchanges O₂ and CO₂. Anatomy: nose/mouth → pharynx → larynx (voice box) → trachea (windpipe, 10-12cm) → bronchi (2, one per lung) → bronchioles → alveoli (~480 million tiny air sacs, surface area ~70 m²). Breathing: diaphragm contracts (flattens down) → thoracic cavity expands → pressure drops → air rushes in (inspiration). Diaphragm relaxes → pressure increases → air pushed out (expiration). At rest: ~12-20 breaths/min, ~0.5L per breath. Lung capacity: total ~6L. Oxygen transport: 98.5% bound to hemoglobin (in red blood cells), 1.5% dissolved in plasma. CO₂ primarily transported as bicarbonate ions. Asthma: airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction. COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease): emphysema + chronic bronchitis, primarily from smoking — irreversible damage. Pneumonia: lung infection causing alveoli to fill with fluid.

The kidneys (two bean-shaped organs, each ~11cm) filter ~180 liters of blood per day, producing ~1.5L of urine. Each kidney has ~1 million nephrons (filtering units). Functions: filter waste (urea, creatinine, excess salts), regulate blood pressure (renin-angiotensin system), maintain fluid/electrolyte balance, produce erythropoietin (stimulates red blood cell production), and activate vitamin D. Urine composition: water (95%), urea, creatinine, uric acid, ions. Kidney stones: crystallized minerals (calcium oxalate most common) — extremely painful passing through ureter. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): affects ~10% of adults globally — diabetes and hypertension are leading causes. Dialysis: artificial kidney filtering — hemodialysis (3×/week, 4 hours/session) or peritoneal dialysis (daily). Kidney transplant is preferred treatment for end-stage renal disease.

Skin is the body's largest organ (~2 m², ~3.6 kg), with three layers: epidermis (outer — dead keratinocytes form waterproof barrier; melanocytes produce melanin pigment; Langerhans cells are immune sentinels), dermis (collagen and elastin fibers for strength/elasticity; hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous/oil glands, nerve endings, blood vessels), hypodermis/subcutaneous (fat layer — insulation, cushioning, energy storage). Skin regenerates every ~2-4 weeks. Wound healing stages: hemostasis (clotting, minutes) → inflammation (days 1-4) → proliferation (new tissue, days 4-21) → remodeling (months-years — scar formation). Melanin: produced by melanocytes, absorbs UV radiation. Darker skin has more melanin — better UV protection. Sunscreen: SPF (Sun Protection Factor) measures UVB blocking — SPF 30 blocks 97%, SPF 50 blocks 98%. UVA rays cause aging; UVB cause burning and melanoma risk.

The endocrine system uses hormones (chemical messengers) to regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction, mood, and homeostasis. Key glands and hormones: Pituitary (master gland — controls others): GH (growth hormone), TSH (thyroid stimulating), FSH/LH (sex hormones), ADH (water retention), oxytocin (bonding, labor). Thyroid: T3/T4 (metabolism rate) — hypothyroidism (too slow, fatigue, weight gain), hyperthyroidism (too fast, weight loss, anxiety). Adrenal glands: cortisol (stress response, inflammation), adrenaline/epinephrine (fight-or-flight), aldosterone (blood pressure). Pancreas: insulin (lowers blood glucose — moves glucose into cells), glucagon (raises blood glucose). Gonads: testosterone (male sex characteristics, muscle, libido — also present in females at lower levels), estrogen and progesterone (female sex characteristics, menstrual cycle, pregnancy). Melatonin (pineal gland): regulates sleep-wake cycle.

The human eye detects light and converts it to neural signals. Anatomy: cornea (transparent outer layer, 65-75% of focusing power) → aqueous humor → iris (controls pupil size/light intake) → lens (adjusts focus — accommodation) → vitreous humor → retina (inner lining with photoreceptors) → optic nerve → visual cortex. Photoreceptors: rods (~120 million, low light/scotopic vision, peripheral) and cones (~6 million, color/photopic vision, concentrated in fovea). Three cone types: L (red, ~564nm), M (green, ~534nm), S (blue, ~420nm). Color blindness: X-linked recessive — affects ~8% of males, ~0.5% of females. Most common: red-green color blindness. Myopia (nearsightedness): eyeball too long, light focuses in front of retina — corrected with concave lenses. Hyperopia (farsightedness): eyeball too short. Astigmatism: irregular cornea curvature. 20/20 vision means seeing at 20 feet what a normal eye sees at 20 feet.

The ear handles hearing and balance. Three parts: outer ear (pinna collects sound → ear canal → eardrum/tympanic membrane vibrates), middle ear (three ossicles — malleus, incus, stapes — amplify vibrations ~20×; Eustachian tube equalizes pressure), inner ear (cochlea — fluid-filled spiral converts vibrations to neural signals via hair cells; vestibular system — semicircular canals detect rotation, otolith organs detect linear acceleration and gravity). Hearing range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (Hz decreases with age — adults often lose high frequencies). Decibel scale (logarithmic): 0 dB (threshold of hearing), 30 dB (whisper), 60 dB (conversation), 85 dB (threshold of damage with prolonged exposure), 120 dB (jet engine, pain threshold), 194 dB (loudest possible sound in atmosphere). Hair cells do NOT regenerate in mammals — hearing loss from noise or age is permanent. Tinnitus (ringing in ears) affects ~15% of adults.

Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of deviation from rational judgment. Key ones: Confirmation bias: seek/interpret information confirming existing beliefs — the most pervasive bias. Availability heuristic: judge probability by how easily examples come to mind (plane crashes feel more common than car crashes because they're more memorable). Anchoring: over-rely on first piece of information (first salary offer anchors negotiations). Dunning-Kruger effect: incompetent people overestimate their ability; experts underestimate theirs relative to novices. Sunk cost fallacy: continue bad decisions because of past investment ('I've spent too much on this to quit'). Loss aversion: losses feel ~2× more painful than equivalent gains feel good (Kahneman & Tversky). Framing effect: same information presented differently changes decisions ('90% survival rate' vs '10% mortality rate'). Hindsight bias: after knowing the outcome, believing you 'knew it all along.' Bandwagon effect: adopt beliefs because others hold them. Status quo bias: prefer things as they are even when change would be better.

Personality psychology attempts to measure stable individual differences. Big Five (OCEAN) — most scientifically validated model: Openness (curiosity, creativity, preference for novelty vs. consistency), Conscientiousness (organization, dependability, self-discipline), Extraversion (sociability, positive emotion, assertiveness — introversion is the opposite end), Agreeableness (cooperation, empathy, trust), Neuroticism (emotional instability, anxiety, moodiness). Each is a spectrum, not a type. Big Five traits are ~40-60% heritable and relatively stable after age 30. Myers-Briggs (MBTI): popular but scientifically weak — low test-retest reliability (~50% of people get a different type 5 weeks later), dichotomies are artificial cuts on continuous dimensions. It remains widely used in business despite academic criticism. Introversion/extraversion: fundamentally about where you get energy (alone vs social settings) not shyness. About 30-50% of people are ambiverts (in the middle).

Trauma is an emotional response to a deeply distressing event that overwhelms the ability to cope. Types: acute (single incident), chronic (repeated — domestic violence, childhood abuse), complex (C-PTSD, prolonged interpersonal trauma), vicarious (from witnessing others' trauma — first responders, therapists). PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder): develops in ~20% of trauma survivors. Symptoms: intrusive memories/flashbacks, nightmares, hypervigilance, avoidance, negative cognitions, emotional numbing. Affects ~3.5% of US adults/year. Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) Study (CDC, 1995-1997): 10 types of childhood trauma (abuse, neglect, household dysfunction). Each ACE increases risk of depression, heart disease, cancer, early death — profound dose-response relationship. 64% of adults had at least 1 ACE; 12.5% had 4+. Resilience: ability to adapt to adversity. Key factors: social support, sense of control/agency, meaning-making, previous coping experience. Effective PTSD treatments: Prolonged Exposure, EMDR, Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT).

Addiction: compulsive substance use or behavior despite harmful consequences, characterized by loss of control, craving, and continued use despite negative effects. The brain's reward system: dopamine released in nucleus accumbens creates pleasurable feelings. Addictive substances hijack this system — cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake (immediate massive surge), opioids bind to opioid receptors, alcohol enhances GABA (inhibitory) and blocks NMDA (excitatory). Tolerance: brain downregulates receptors — need more to get the same effect. Dependence: brain adapts and requires substance to function normally. Withdrawal: rebound when substance is removed — can be fatal for alcohol and benzodiazepines (seizures). Classes: alcohol, opioids (heroin, fentanyl — fentanyl 100× more potent than morphine, responsible for overdose epidemic), stimulants (cocaine, meth, amphetamines), cannabis, sedatives, hallucinogens, nicotine. Behavioral addictions: gambling, gaming, pornography (controversial). Treatment: MAT (Medication-Assisted Treatment) — methadone, buprenorphine for opioids — most effective for opioid use disorder. AA/12-step programs, CBT, inpatient/outpatient rehab.

Child development covers physical, cognitive, social, and emotional growth. Jean Piaget's cognitive development stages: Sensorimotor (0-2 years — object permanence develops; understanding things exist when out of sight), Preoperational (2-7 years — symbolic thinking, egocentrism, animism; lack of conservation — same amount of water looks different in differently shaped glasses), Concrete Operational (7-11 years — logical thinking about concrete objects, conservation mastered), Formal Operational (12+ years — abstract reasoning, hypothetical thinking). Lev Vygotsky: Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) — the gap between what a child can do alone vs. with guidance. Scaffolding bridges this gap. John Bowlby's attachment theory: early caregiver bonds shape emotional development. Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation: Secure (66%), Anxious-Ambivalent, Avoidant, Disorganized attachment styles. Secure attachment predicts better outcomes. Language development: babbling (6-8 months), first words (10-14 months), two-word combinations (18-24 months), complex sentences (3-4 years). Critical period for language acquisition: before puberty.

The American Civil Rights Movement (1954-1968) fought to end racial segregation and discrimination against Black Americans. Jim Crow laws: state/local laws enforcing racial segregation in the South after Reconstruction (1877-1950s). Key events: Brown v. Board of Education (1954, Supreme Court — 'separate but equal' schools unconstitutional), Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat, 381-day boycott led by Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.), Little Rock Nine (1957, nine Black students integrated Central High School with federal troops), Greensboro sit-ins (1960, four Black college students at Woolworth's lunch counter), Freedom Riders (1961), March on Washington (August 28, 1963, MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech, 250,000 people), Civil Rights Act of 1964 (banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin), Voting Rights Act of 1965, MLK assassinated April 4, 1968. The movement used nonviolent civil disobedience inspired by Gandhi.

The Holocaust (Hebrew: Shoah — 'catastrophe') was the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of 6 million Jews (two-thirds of European Jewry) and 5-6 million others (Roma, disabled people, Soviet POWs, political opponents, LGBTQ+ people) by the Nazi regime under Adolf Hitler (1933-1945). The 'Final Solution': decision to exterminate all Jews (Wannsee Conference, January 1942). Death camps (Operation Reinhard): Auschwitz-Birkenau (largest — 1.1 million Jews killed), Treblinka (700,000-900,000), Belzec, Sobibor, Chelmno, Majdanek — all in occupied Poland. Methods: gas chambers (Zyklon B at Auschwitz), shooting (Einsatzgruppen mobile killing units — 1.5+ million Jews), starvation, overwork. Elie Wiesel (Night), Anne Frank (The Diary of a Young Girl) — key survivor testimonies. Nuremberg Trials (1945-46) established the legal framework for crimes against humanity. 'Never Again' — the imperative of Holocaust remembrance.

Apartheid (Afrikaans: 'separateness') was South Africa's system of institutionalized racial segregation and white supremacy (1948-1994). Laws classified people as White, Coloured, Indian, or Black. Black South Africans (80% of population) could not vote, were forced into 'homelands' (Bantustans), required to carry passbooks, and were excluded from skilled jobs, quality schools, and public facilities. The African National Congress (ANC, founded 1912) led resistance. Key events: Sharpeville Massacre (1960 — police killed 69 protesters, ANC banned), Soweto Uprising (June 16, 1976 — students shot protesting Afrikaans-only teaching). Nelson Mandela: ANC leader imprisoned for 27 years (1964-1990) on Robben Island for sabotage. Became South Africa's first Black president after the first democratic elections (1994). F.W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC and released Mandela — both won the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize. Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC): restorative justice process hearing testimonies of human rights violations.

The Vietnam War (1955-1975, US involvement 1964-1975) was a Cold War conflict between communist North Vietnam (Viet Cong, supported by USSR and China) and South Vietnam (supported by the USA). US justification: Domino Theory — if one country fell to communism, neighboring countries would follow. Gulf of Tonkin incident (August 1964): alleged attacks on US destroyers led Congress to authorize military action (later found to be exaggerated/fabricated). US troop peak: 543,000 (1969). Draft: conscription of ~2.2 million Americans — protests led to lottery system. Tet Offensive (January 1968): surprise coordinated attacks on 100+ cities — military failure for North Vietnam but psychological turning point, showing the war was far from won. My Lai Massacre (1968): US troops killed 347-504 unarmed South Vietnamese civilians. Anti-war movement grew. Nixon's 'Vietnamization' — withdrawing US troops. Fall of Saigon (April 30, 1975). Deaths: ~58,000 Americans, ~1.1-1.5 million North/South Vietnamese military, ~2 million+ civilians. Agent Orange (herbicide/defoliant): caused birth defects in Vietnamese and health problems in US veterans.

The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is one of the world's most complex and enduring. Zionism: late 19th-century movement for Jewish homeland in historic Palestine, driven by European antisemitism (Theodor Herzl). British Mandate Palestine (1920-1948) saw competing Jewish and Arab nationalisms. UN Partition Plan (1947): proposed dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states, with Jerusalem under international control. Israel declared independence May 14, 1948 — Arabs call this al-Nakba ('the Catastrophe') as ~700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. Israel-Arab Wars: 1948-49 (Israeli War of Independence), 1956 (Suez Crisis), 1967 Six-Day War (Israel captured West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, Golan Heights), 1973 Yom Kippur War. Oslo Accords (1993): Palestinian Authority established, framework for peace — stalled. Gaza: Hamas (designated terrorist organization by US/EU) took control 2007 — blockaded by Israel and Egypt. West Bank: Israeli settlements (illegal under international law per most interpretations) continue to expand. Two-state solution remains the international consensus but has not been achieved.

Decolonization: the process by which colonies gained independence from European powers, primarily after WWII. Asia: India and Pakistan independence August 14-15, 1947 (Partition — one of history's largest forced migrations, ~14 million displaced, ~1 million killed in communal violence). Indonesia (1945/1949 from Netherlands), Vietnam (1954 from France after First Indochina War). Africa: 'Year of Africa' 1960 — 17 countries gained independence. Most sub-Saharan African nations became independent 1957-1980. The 'Scramble for Africa' (Berlin Conference 1884-85): European powers divided Africa drawing straight lines on maps ignoring ethnic, linguistic, and religious boundaries — creating artificial nations that have caused conflicts ever since. The Congo: Belgian Congo became DRC (1960) — immediate chaos (Patrice Lumumba assassination, CIA involvement, Mobutu dictatorship). Zimbabwe: white minority rule ended 1980. South Africa: apartheid ended 1994. Colonial legacy: economic underdevelopment, resource extraction without reinvestment, educational deprivation, ethnic tensions from arbitrary borders, and psychological impact of cultural suppression.

Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support ~25% of all marine species — called 'the rainforests of the sea.' Corals are animals (polyps) with a mutualistic relationship with photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) that live in their tissue and provide up to 90% of their energy. Coral bleaching: when ocean temperatures rise even 1-2°C above summer maximums, corals expel their zooxanthellae — turning white. Prolonged bleaching kills corals. Great Barrier Reef: experienced mass bleaching events in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 — 50%+ of shallow water corals died. Ocean acidification: oceans absorb ~25% of CO₂ emissions → forms carbonic acid → lowers pH (now 8.1 vs. pre-industrial 8.2 — 30% more acidic). This weakens coral skeletons and shellfish. At current trends, most coral reefs will be functionally extinct by 2050. Reef restoration: coral gardening, assisted gene flow (breeding heat-resistant corals), and solar radiation management are being explored. Reefs provide ~$375 billion/year in goods and services to 1 billion people.

The IUCN Red List classifies species by extinction risk: Extinct (EX), Extinct in the Wild (EW), Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN), Vulnerable (VU), Near Threatened (NT), Least Concern (LC). As of 2024: ~44,000+ species threatened with extinction out of ~150,000 assessed. The 6th mass extinction: current extinction rate is 100-1,000× higher than background rates — comparable to the 5 previous mass extinctions. Driven by: habitat destruction (primary driver — deforestation, agriculture, urbanization), overexploitation (hunting, fishing), invasive species, pollution, climate change, and disease. Most endangered: Amur leopard (~100 left), Javan rhino (~70), Sumatran orangutan (~14,000), mountain gorilla (~1,100). Conservation success stories: bald eagle (removed from endangered list 2007), humpback whale (populations recovering), Arabian oryx (returned from extinct in the wild). Edward O. Wilson estimated ~8 million species exist on Earth; only ~2 million have been named.

Wildfires are uncontrolled fires burning through vegetation. They are natural and essential in many ecosystems — fire-adapted plants (sequoias, lodgepole pines) need fire to reproduce. Fire triangle: fuel (dry vegetation), heat (lightning, human ignition), oxygen. Climate change is making wildfires worse: higher temperatures → drier vegetation → longer fire seasons. Notable events: 2019-20 Australian bushfires ('Black Summer') — 18.6 million hectares burned, 3 billion animals affected, 34 people killed, smoke encircled the globe. 2020 California fires — worst in state history, 4 million acres burned. Amazon fires (annual peak Aug-Sep) — set deliberately for agriculture, destroying irreplaceable rainforest. Canada 2023: worst fire season ever — 18 million hectares, smoke blanketed eastern US. Prescribed/controlled burning: intentional burning under controlled conditions to reduce fuel loads — practiced by Indigenous peoples for thousands of years, increasingly adopted by land managers.

Plastic production: 400+ million tonnes/year (2022), up from 2 million tonnes in 1950. Cumulative production: 9.2 billion tonnes. Only 9% has ever been recycled; 12% incinerated; 79% in landfills or environment. Single-use plastics account for ~50% of all plastic produced. Ocean plastic: 8-12 million tonnes enter oceans annually. Great Pacific Garbage Patch: ~1.6 million km², mostly microplastics — not a solid island, more like a plastic soup. Rivers transport plastic to ocean — 10 rivers (8 in Asia, 2 in Africa) carry ~90% of river-borne ocean plastic. Microplastics (<5mm): found everywhere on Earth — Mariana Trench, Arctic snow, cloud water, human lungs, blood, placentas, breast milk. Health effects: under active research — some chemicals (phthalates, BPA) are endocrine disruptors. Plastic takes 20-500 years to break down — it photodegrades into smaller pieces but doesn't disappear. Solutions: ban single-use plastics (EU, many countries), extended producer responsibility, better waste management in developing countries, improved recycling technology.

Agriculture: ~10,000 years old, began in the Fertile Crescent (wheat, barley), Yangtze Valley (rice), and Mesoamerica (corn/maize). Today covers ~50% of Earth's habitable land — the single largest land use. Green Revolution (1960s-70s): Norman Borlaug developed high-yield wheat varieties, saving an estimated 1 billion lives from famine — Nobel Peace Prize 1970. GMOs (Genetically Modified Organisms): organisms with DNA altered using genetic engineering. ~90% of US corn and soybeans are GMO. Scientific consensus: safe for consumption (WHO, National Academies of Sciences). Benefits: pest resistance, drought tolerance, enhanced nutrition (Golden Rice: vitamin A). Concerns: corporate control (Monsanto/Bayer), ecological effects, farmer dependence. Organic farming: no synthetic pesticides/fertilizers, typically 20-25% lower yields. Yields: conventional agriculture produces ~3× more food per hectare than organic. Food waste: ~1/3 of all food produced (~1.3 billion tonnes) is wasted annually — if food waste were a country, it would be the 3rd largest greenhouse gas emitter. Factory farming: ~70 billion land animals raised for food annually — serious animal welfare and antibiotic resistance concerns.

Global development: World Bank classifies countries as low-income (<$1,135 GNI/capita), lower-middle, upper-middle, and high-income (>$13,845). Extreme poverty: <$2.15/day — declined from 36% (1990) to 9% (2022), but COVID-19 reversed progress for first time in 20 years. About 700 million still in extreme poverty, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The IMF (International Monetary Fund, 190 members): lends to countries in financial crises, conditional on economic reforms ('structural adjustment programs' — controversial for imposing austerity). World Bank: provides loans and grants for development projects. Aid effectiveness debate: Jeffrey Sachs (Big Push — massive aid can end poverty), William Easterly (aid creates dependency, local solutions better), Dambisa Moyo (Dead Aid — aid has harmed Africa). Effective altruism: use evidence to maximize good — GiveWell recommends highest-impact charities. Human Development Index (HDI): composite of life expectancy, education, and income per capita. Top countries: Norway, Switzerland, Iceland. Bottom: South Sudan, Chad, Niger.

Taxation funds government services. Types: Income tax (progressive in most countries — higher rates on higher income). Corporate tax (on company profits). VAT/sales tax (on goods and services — regressive, hits lower incomes harder as % of spending). Property tax (on real estate value). Capital gains tax (on investment profits). Inheritance/estate tax (on wealth transferred at death). Payroll tax (Social Security, Medicare in USA). Tax avoidance (legal — using deductions, offshore structures) vs. tax evasion (illegal — hiding income). Top US marginal tax rates historically: 94% (1944), 91% (1950s), 50% (Reagan, then cut to 28% 1988), ~37% currently. The Laffer Curve: there's an optimal tax rate — too high reduces economic activity; revenue doesn't always increase with higher rates. Tax havens: countries with low/zero taxes — Cayman Islands, Luxembourg, Ireland, Netherlands — used by corporations and wealthy individuals. The global minimum corporate tax (15%, OECD, 2021): attempt to end this race to the bottom.

Feminism: movement for equal political, economic, social, and personal rights for women. Waves: First wave (late 19th-early 20th century): women's suffrage — Seneca Falls Convention (1848, 'all men and women are created equal'), UK women's vote (1918, over 30), US 19th Amendment (1920). Second wave (1960s-80s): beyond voting rights — reproductive rights (Roe v. Wade 1973, overturned 2022), workplace equality, domestic violence laws. Second Shift: women work full time AND do majority of domestic labor. The Feminine Mystique (Betty Friedan, 1963). Third wave (1990s-2000s): intersectionality (Kimberlé Crenshaw — race, class, gender intertwine), reclaiming femininity, challenging binaries. MeToo movement (2017, Tarana Burke coined the phrase; viral after Harvey Weinstein exposé): sexual harassment and assault. Gender pay gap: US women earn ~82 cents per dollar men earn — partly explained by occupation and hours, partly by discrimination. Global gender parity: World Economic Forum estimates ~130 years to close the global gender gap at current rates. Women's suffrage worldwide: Saudi Arabia (2015), Switzerland (1971), France (1944).

Immigration: people moving permanently or semi-permanently to another country. Types: economic migrants (seeking better opportunities), refugees (fleeing persecution — protected by 1951 UN Refugee Convention), asylum seekers (applied for but haven't received refugee status), internally displaced people (IDPs — fled violence within own country). UNHCR: 110 million+ people forcibly displaced worldwide as of 2023 — highest ever. Top refugee-hosting countries: Iran, Turkey, Pakistan, Uganda (not wealthy Western nations). US immigration: ~1 million legal immigrants/year, ~10.5-11 million undocumented immigrants (declined from 12.2 million in 2007). DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, 2012): protected ~800,000 'Dreamers' brought to US as children. Ellis Island (1892-1954): processed ~12 million immigrants. Push/pull factors: push (war, poverty, climate change), pull (jobs, family, stability). Economic research consensus: immigration broadly benefits receiving economies — immigrants pay taxes, start businesses, and fill labor shortages.

Viruses vs. bacteria: Viruses (~20-300nm) are not technically alive — they're genetic material (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat, requiring a host cell to replicate. They hijack cell machinery to copy themselves, often destroying the cell. Antibiotics have NO effect on viruses. Antiviral drugs target viral processes — fewer available than antibiotics. Bacteria (~1-10 micrometers) are living single-celled organisms — most are harmless or beneficial (gut microbiome). Antibiotics kill/inhibit bacteria by targeting cell walls, protein synthesis, or DNA replication. COVID-19: caused by SARS-CoV-2 (a coronavirus — named for crown-like spike proteins). Identified December 2019 in Wuhan, China. WHO declared pandemic March 11, 2020. Global deaths: officially ~7 million, estimated excess deaths 15-20 million. Influenza: RNA virus, mutates rapidly (why annual flu shots needed). 1918 Spanish Flu: killed 50-100 million (3-5% of world population) — most lethal pandemic in recorded history. HIV: attacks CD4+ T cells (helper T cells) — destroys immune system. No cure but antiretroviral therapy (ART) allows normal lifespan. ~38 million people living with HIV.

Plants (kingdom Plantae): ~390,000 species. Divided into: non-vascular (mosses, liverworts — no water transport system), vascular seedless (ferns), seed plants (gymnosperms — conifers, cycads; angiosperms — flowering plants, 90%+ of plant species). The oldest living organism: Pando, a quaking aspen colony in Utah, ~80,000 years old, 6 million kg. Tallest tree: Hyperion (coast redwood, 115.7m). Oldest individual tree: Great Basin bristlecone pine 'Methuselah,' ~4,800 years old. Fungi (kingdom Fungi): not plants — no photosynthesis, digest food externally, cell walls made of chitin. 3 million+ species estimated. Mycorrhizal networks: ~90% of land plants form symbiotic relationships with fungi — fungi extend roots' reach for water and nutrients, plants provide sugars. The 'Wood Wide Web': forest trees connected by fungal networks, sharing nutrients and chemical signals. The largest organism on Earth: Armillaria honey fungus in Oregon — ~9.6 km², ~2,400 years old.

Space weather describes conditions in space that affect Earth's technology and environment. Solar flares: sudden intense bursts of radiation from the Sun's surface — travel at the speed of light (reach Earth in 8 minutes). Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs): massive clouds of magnetized plasma ejected from the Sun — take 1-3 days to reach Earth. Effects: disrupt satellite communications, GPS, radio, and power grids. Auroras (Northern/Southern Lights): CMEs interact with Earth's magnetic field → energize atmospheric particles → glow at polar regions (oxygen: green/red, nitrogen: blue/purple). Visible further from poles during intense solar activity. The Carrington Event (September 1-2, 1859): the most powerful geomagnetic storm in recorded history — telegraph systems failed, operators received electric shocks, northern lights seen as far south as Cuba. If a Carrington-level event hit today: could destroy transformers globally, causing power outages lasting months-years and trillions of dollars in damage. Solar cycle: ~11-year cycle of solar activity (sunspot minimum to maximum). Solar Cycle 25 peaked 2024-2025.

Nanotechnology: manipulation of matter at the nanoscale (1-100 nanometers — a human hair is ~80,000nm wide). At this scale, materials have different properties than their bulk forms. Carbon nanotubes: cylinders of carbon atoms, 100× stronger than steel at 1/6 the weight, excellent electrical conductors — potential applications in composites, electronics, medicine. Graphene: single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal lattice — strongest material ever tested (200× stronger than steel), excellent conductor of heat and electricity, one atom thick. Discovered 2004 by Geim and Novoselov (2010 Nobel Prize) using Scotch tape on graphite. Nanomedicine applications: targeted drug delivery (nanoparticles deliver drugs directly to cancer cells, reducing side effects), diagnostic imaging, antibacterial coatings, wound healing. Sunscreens already use zinc oxide and titanium dioxide nanoparticles. Environmental concerns: nanoparticles may be toxic — size makes them able to cross biological barriers (blood-brain barrier). The global nanotechnology market: ~$100 billion/year.

Emoji: pictograms used in digital communication. Originally created by Shigetaka Kurita for NTT DoCoMo in Japan in 1999 (176 emoji). Unicode Consortium standardizes emoji globally. Over 3,600 emoji in Unicode 15.1 (2023). The most used emoji: 😂 (Face with Tears of Joy) — consistently #1 globally. 'Emoji' is both singular and plural (Japanese word). Internet memes: ideas/behaviors/styles spreading virally online. Term from Richard Dawkins' 'The Selfish Gene' (1976) — cultural information units spreading like genes. First internet memes: Dancing Baby (1996), All Your Base Are Belong To Us (2001), LOLcats/I Can Has Cheezburger? (2007). Know Your Meme documents meme history. Gen Z slang (born ~1997-2012): 'no cap' (no lie), 'bussin' (really good), 'slay' (doing great), 'vibe check,' 'rent free' (occupying your thoughts), 'understood the assignment,' 'it's giving,' 'lowkey/highkey,' 'based' (holding unpopular opinion unapologetically), 'mid' (mediocre), 'sus' (suspicious, from Among Us).

Fashion industry: ~$1.7 trillion global market. Luxury fashion houses: LVMH (Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy — world's largest luxury conglomerate, owns LV, Dior, Givenchy, Fendi, Bulgari, Sephora, Dom Pérignon, Veuve Clicquot), Kering (Gucci, Saint Laurent, Bottega Veneta, Balenciaga), Richemont (Cartier, IWC, Jaeger-LeCoultre). Fast fashion: Zara (Inditex — designs to stores in 2 weeks, 20 collections/year), H&M, SHEIN (Chinese, ultra-fast, $3-10 items, accused of copying independent designers). Environmental impact: fashion is the 2nd most polluting industry (after oil). Produces 10% of global carbon emissions, uses 93 billion cubic meters of water/year, generates 21 billion tons of textile waste annually. Polyester (plastic — 60% of clothing): doesn't biodegrade, sheds microplastics. Fast fashion workers: predominantly women in Bangladesh, Cambodia, Vietnam earning $3-5/day. Rana Plaza collapse (2013, Bangladesh): 1,134 garment workers killed — watershed moment for ethical fashion. Sustainable fashion: secondhand (ThredUp, Depop, Vinted), rental (Rent the Runway), brands using recycled materials.

Gastronomy: the art and science of good eating. Street food: $180 billion global market, integral to culture in Asia (Bangkok hawker stalls, Japanese ramen shops, Mexican tacos), Middle East (shawarma, falafel), and Latin America. Michelin Guide: published by tire company Michelin since 1900 (originally to encourage driving and tire wear). Stars: 1 star (very good), 2 stars (worth a detour), 3 stars (worth a special journey). 3-star restaurants worldwide: ~150. Joël Robuchon had 32 Michelin stars — most ever. Famous chefs: Julia Child (brought French cuisine to America), Escoffier (codified classical French cuisine), Ferran Adrià (elBulli — molecular gastronomy/avant-garde), René Redzepi (Noma, Copenhagen — New Nordic cuisine, world's best restaurant multiple times), Gordon Ramsay (17 Michelin stars), Heston Blumenthal (The Fat Duck — science-inspired). Fermentation: one of humanity's oldest preservation techniques — kimchi (Korean, UNESCO intangible heritage), miso, sourdough, cheese, wine, beer, sauerkraut, tempeh, natto. Umami: fifth basic taste (alongside sweet, sour, salty, bitter), discovered by Kikunae Ikeda (1908) — glutamate triggers it.

Sports science applies scientific principles to athletic performance. Key areas: Exercise physiology (VO₂ max — maximum oxygen uptake, best predictor of aerobic performance; lactate threshold — intensity at which lactic acid accumulates faster than cleared), Biomechanics (efficient movement mechanics), Nutrition (carbohydrate loading before endurance events, protein timing for muscle synthesis), Psychology (visualization, flow state — Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's concept of optimal performance), Recovery (sleep is the most important, ice baths debated, foam rolling helps). Altitude training: lower O₂ at altitude → body produces more red blood cells → better O₂ transport at sea level. Elite athletes train at 2,000-3,000m. Doping in sport: WADA (World Anti-Doping Agency, 1999) oversees testing. Banned substances: EPO (erythropoietin — blood doping), human growth hormone, anabolic steroids, stimulants, blood transfusions. Lance Armstrong stripped of 7 Tour de France titles (2012) for systematic doping. Russia state-sponsored doping program (Sochi 2014) — banned from competing under Russian flag. The 'pharmacological arms race' continues.

Web accessibility (a11y — 11 letters between 'a' and 'y') ensures websites are usable by people with disabilities. ~1 billion people (15% of world population) have some form of disability. WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) 2.1 — four principles (POUR): Perceivable (text alternatives for images, captions for video, sufficient color contrast ≥4.5:1 for normal text), Operable (keyboard accessible, no seizure-inducing content, enough time to read), Understandable (readable text, predictable behavior, error assistance), Robust (compatible with assistive technologies). Levels: A (minimum), AA (standard — most legal requirements), AAA (enhanced). Screen readers: NVDA (free, Windows), JAWS (Windows), VoiceOver (macOS/iOS built-in), TalkBack (Android built-in). ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications): HTML attributes that provide semantic information to assistive technologies — aria-label, aria-describedby, role, aria-live. Legal requirements: ADA (USA), EN 301 549 (EU), Equality Act (UK). Inaccessible websites are subject to lawsuits — 4,000+ ADA web lawsuits in 2023 (USA).

Web performance directly impacts user experience and revenue — Amazon found every 100ms of latency costs 1% in sales. Core Web Vitals (Google, used in search ranking): LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, <2.5s — loading), FID (First Input Delay, <100ms — interactivity, replaced by INP in 2024), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, <0.1 — visual stability). Tools: Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools — audit tool), WebPageTest, PageSpeed Insights, GTmetrix. Optimization techniques: Image optimization (WebP/AVIF format, lazy loading, proper sizing), Code splitting (only load JS needed for current page), Minification (remove whitespace/comments), GZIP/Brotli compression, Critical CSS (inline above-fold CSS), Preloading/prefetching, Caching (browser cache, service workers), CDN (Content Delivery Network — Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai — serve content from servers near the user). The performance budget: set maximum sizes for page assets and test against it in CI/CD.

Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) are web apps that use modern browser APIs to provide app-like experiences. Key features: Installable (Add to Home Screen — appears like a native app, no app store needed), Offline capability (Service Worker: a JavaScript proxy that intercepts network requests, caches responses, and serves cached content when offline), Push notifications (browser push API, works even when app isn't open), Fast (pre-cached assets load instantly), Responsive (works on all screen sizes), Secure (HTTPS required). Service Worker lifecycle: install → activate → fetch events. Cache strategies: Cache First (serve cached, update background), Network First (try network, fallback to cache), Stale While Revalidate (serve cache, update in background simultaneously). PWA examples: Twitter Lite (data usage reduced 70%), Pinterest (40% more time spent), Starbucks (99.84% smaller than native app). Web App Manifest (manifest.json): defines app name, icons, colors, start URL, display mode. Limitations vs native: no access to some device APIs, push notifications less reliable on iOS (improved in iOS 16.4+).

Regular expressions (regex/regexp) are patterns for matching, searching, and manipulating text. Core syntax: . (any character except newline), * (0+ repetitions), + (1+ repetitions), ? (0 or 1), ^ (start of string), $ (end of string), [] (character class), [^] (negated class), | (alternation/or), () (group), {} (specific count: {3} exactly 3, {2,5} between 2-5). Common character classes: \d (digit [0-9]), \w (word character [a-zA-Z0-9_]), \s (whitespace), \D \W \S (negated). Greedy vs. lazy: .* matches as much as possible (greedy); .*? matches as little as possible (lazy). Lookahead: (?=...) positive, (?!...) negative. Lookbehind: (?<=...) positive, (?<!...) negative. Useful patterns: Email: /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/, URL: /https?:\/\/(www\.)?[-a-zA-Z0-9@:%._+~#=]{1,256}\.[a-zA-Z0-9()]{1,6}/, Phone (US): /^(\+1)?[2-9]\d{2}[2-9]\d{6}$/. Test regex interactively at regex101.com.

API design best practices: Use nouns for resources (/users, /products), not verbs (/getUsers). Plural resource names (/users not /user). HTTP methods semantically (GET=read, POST=create, PUT=replace, PATCH=partial update, DELETE=remove). Consistent error responses: always return error object with code, message, and possibly details. Versioning strategies: URL path (/api/v1/users — most common, clear), query param (?version=1), header (Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json — cleanest but harder to test). Pagination: offset/limit (?offset=20&limit=10), cursor-based (for large/real-time data — more reliable). Rate limiting: return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header. Include limit/remaining/reset in response headers. Documentation: OpenAPI/Swagger spec — generate interactive docs automatically. Idempotency: PUT/DELETE/GET should produce same result regardless of how many times called. Authentication: JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for stateless auth, OAuth 2.0 for third-party authorization. HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State): responses include links to related actions — makes APIs self-documenting.

Periodic table trends across periods (left to right): atomic radius decreases (more protons pull electrons closer), ionization energy increases (harder to remove electrons — more protons hold them tighter), electronegativity increases (Pauling scale — F=3.98, most electronegative element), electron affinity generally increases. Down a group: atomic radius increases (more electron shells), ionization energy decreases, electronegativity decreases. Electronegativity drives bond type: >1.7 difference = ionic bond (NaCl), <1.7 = covalent bond. When two atoms of same element bond = nonpolar covalent. Metallic character decreases across a period, increases down a group. Metalloids (Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) sit on the 'staircase' boundary between metals and nonmetals — semiconductor behavior.

Chemical reaction types: Synthesis (A+B→AB), Decomposition (AB→A+B), Single displacement (A+BC→AC+B), Double displacement (AB+CD→AD+CB), Combustion (fuel+O₂→CO₂+H₂O+energy), Acid-Base neutralization. Redox reactions: electron transfer. Oxidation = loss of electrons (OIL: Oxidation Is Loss). Reduction = gain of electrons (RIG: Reduction Is Gain). Oxidizing agent takes electrons; reducing agent gives them. pH scale (0-14): measures H⁺ ion concentration. pH = -log[H⁺]. pH 7 = neutral (pure water). Below 7 = acidic (higher H⁺). Above 7 = alkaline/basic (lower H⁺, higher OH⁻). Each pH unit = 10× difference in acidity. Stomach acid: pH 1.5-3.5 (extremely acidic). Blood: pH 7.35-7.45 (maintained tightly — acidosis or alkalosis are medical emergencies). Strong acids fully dissociate (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃). Buffers resist pH changes — bicarbonate buffer system maintains blood pH.

Materials science bridges physics, chemistry, and engineering. Metals: metallic bonding (electrons delocalized — 'sea of electrons' explains conductivity, malleability, luster). Alloys: mixtures of metals — steel (iron+carbon, 10× stronger than iron), bronze (copper+tin, Bronze Age), brass (copper+zinc), aluminum alloys (aerospace). Semiconductors: conductivity between metals and insulators, tunable by doping (adding impurities — n-type: extra electrons; p-type: electron holes). Silicon is the dominant semiconductor. Polymers: long chains of repeating monomers. Natural (rubber, cellulose, proteins, DNA) vs synthetic (polyethylene, PVC, nylon, Kevlar, carbon fiber). Ceramics: inorganic, non-metallic, crystalline — extremely hard and heat-resistant but brittle (alumina, silicon carbide, zirconia, porcelain). Superconductors: zero electrical resistance below critical temperature. BCS theory (1957 Nobel). Room-temperature superconductivity: holy grail of materials science — would revolutionize energy transmission, computing, and transportation. LK-99 (2023): claimed room-temperature superconductor, NOT replicated.

The nervous system: Central (brain + spinal cord) and Peripheral (somatic — voluntary movement; autonomic — involuntary: sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' and parasympathetic 'rest-and-digest'). Neurons: cell body (soma) → dendrites (receive signals) → axon (transmit signal) → synaptic terminals. Action potential: ~70mV resting potential → depolarization (Na⁺ rushes in) → repolarization (K⁺ rushes out) → propagates down axon at 70-120 m/s (myelinated). Synapse: signal crosses gap via neurotransmitters (acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, GABA, glutamate). Neurological disorders: Alzheimer's disease (~60-70% of dementia cases — plaques of amyloid-beta and tau tangles destroy neurons, starting in hippocampus; no cure; drugs slow progression slightly). Parkinson's disease: loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra → motor symptoms (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia). L-DOPA treatment. Multiple sclerosis (MS): immune system attacks myelin sheaths. ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease): progressive motor neuron destruction. Stroke: interrupted blood supply to brain (ischemic: clot; hemorrhagic: bleed) — 'FAST' (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911).

Our solar system: 8 planets, 5 dwarf planets (Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Ceres), 290+ moons, millions of asteroids, billions of comets. Inner rocky planets: Mercury (no atmosphere, extreme temperature swings −180°C to 430°C, 88-day year), Venus (hottest planet 462°C average — greenhouse effect from CO₂ atmosphere, rotates backward, day longer than year). Asteroid Belt: between Mars and Jupiter — mainly rocky/metallic debris. Jupiter and Saturn's gravity prevented a planet forming. The Kuiper Belt: beyond Neptune (~30-50 AU) — icy bodies including Pluto, Eris, comets. The Oort Cloud: ~2,000-100,000 AU — theoretical shell of icy objects, source of long-period comets. Voyager 1 (launched 1977): entered interstellar space 2012 — ~160 AU from Sun. New Horizons: flew past Pluto 2015 (discovered heart-shaped nitrogen ice plain Tombaugh Regio), now heading into Kuiper Belt. Comets: dirty snowballs of ice and rock. Halley's Comet: 75-76 year period, last visible 1986, returns 2061.

Optics: the study of light behavior. Light is an electromagnetic wave AND a stream of photons (wave-particle duality). Speed of light in vacuum: 299,792,458 m/s (exactly, by definition). Refraction: light bends when passing between media of different refractive indices (Snell's law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂). Rainbows: water droplets refract AND reflect sunlight, separating wavelengths — red (longest, ~700nm) on outside, violet (shortest, ~400nm) on inside. Total internal reflection: when light hits interface at angle greater than critical angle, it reflects back — basis of fiber optics. Fiber optics: light pulses travel through glass/plastic fibers via total internal reflection — low signal loss, immune to electromagnetic interference, foundation of internet infrastructure. Lasers (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation): coherent, monochromatic, collimated light. Types: CO₂ (cutting), Nd:YAG (medical), semiconductor diode (consumer electronics). Applications: surgery, communications (fiber optic), barcode scanners, printers, LIDAR (self-driving cars), weapons, scientific research.

Cryptography secures communications. Symmetric encryption (same key to encrypt/decrypt): AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard) — the global standard for data at rest. Key must be securely shared. Fast. Asymmetric/Public key encryption: mathematically related key pair — anything encrypted with public key can only be decrypted with private key. RSA: security based on difficulty of factoring large numbers (product of two large primes). ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography): smaller keys, same security as RSA. Diffie-Hellman key exchange: securely establish shared secret over public channel. TLS uses this. Hash functions: one-way — any input → fixed-length output; impossible to reverse; any change in input completely changes output ('avalanche effect'). MD5 (broken), SHA-1 (broken), SHA-256 (secure). Used for: password storage (bcrypt, Argon2 are better — slow by design), file integrity, digital signatures, blockchain. Digital signatures: sign with private key, verify with public key — proves authorship without revealing private key. PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) encrypts email. Quantum computers threaten RSA/ECC — NIST is standardizing post-quantum cryptography (2022-2024).

Graph theory studies networks of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Types: directed (edges have direction — Twitter follow), undirected (Facebook friendship), weighted (edges have values — road distances), unweighted. Trees: connected acyclic graphs (no cycles). Spanning tree: connects all nodes with minimum edges. Minimum spanning tree algorithms: Kruskal's, Prim's. Shortest path algorithms: Dijkstra's (non-negative weights, O((V+E)logV)), Bellman-Ford (handles negative weights), A* (informed search with heuristic — faster than Dijkstra's in practice). Graph traversal: BFS (Breadth-First Search — level by level, finds shortest path in unweighted graphs), DFS (Depth-First Search — goes deep first, finds connected components, detects cycles, topological sort). Real applications: Google Maps (shortest path, traffic weights), social networks (friend recommendations via mutual connections), internet routing (OSPF protocol uses Dijkstra's), compiler optimization (dependency resolution). Six degrees of separation: any two people on Earth are connected by ≤6 social links (small-world property of social networks).

Neural network fundamentals: Input layer → hidden layers → output layer. Each neuron: weighted sum of inputs → activation function → output. Training: Forward pass (predict) → calculate loss (MSE for regression, cross-entropy for classification) → Backward pass (backpropagation — chain rule calculates gradient of loss with respect to each weight) → Gradient descent updates weights (w = w - learning_rate × gradient). Challenges: Vanishing gradients (deep networks — ReLU activation helps), Exploding gradients (gradient clipping), Overfitting (model memorizes training data, poor generalization — regularization: L1/L2 weight penalty; Dropout: randomly zero out neurons during training; early stopping; data augmentation). CNN (Convolutional Neural Network): for grid data (images) — convolutional layers learn spatial features (edges, textures, objects), pooling layers reduce dimensionality. ResNet (2015): residual connections ('skip connections') enabled training of very deep networks (152 layers). RNN (Recurrent Neural Network): for sequential data — hidden state carries context. LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory): gates solve the vanishing gradient problem in RNNs.

The Transformer ('Attention Is All You Need,' Vaswani et al., Google, 2017): the architecture behind all modern LLMs. Key innovation: self-attention mechanism — each token attends to all other tokens in the input, weighted by relevance. Multi-head attention: multiple attention heads learn different types of relationships. Positional encoding: since transformers process all tokens in parallel (unlike RNNs), positional information is explicitly added. Pre-training → fine-tuning paradigm: pre-train on massive unlabeled text corpus (predict next token — autoregressive, or masked tokens — BERT), then fine-tune on specific tasks. BERT (Google, 2018): bidirectional, masked language model — sees context on both sides. GPT series (OpenAI): autoregressive (predicts next token), causal (only attends to previous tokens). Scaling laws (Chinchilla, DeepMind): model performance scales predictably with data and compute — optimal training: scale data and parameters proportionally. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): fine-tune with human preference data to make models helpful and harmless. Constitutional AI (Anthropic): uses AI feedback guided by principles instead of human feedback for each example.

Major rivers of the world: Amazon (South America): world's largest by volume — discharges ~20% of all freshwater entering the world's oceans, 6,400 km long (shorter than Nile but vastly larger watershed of 7 million km²), drains the Amazon rainforest, flows through Brazil and Peru. Nile (Africa): historically considered the world's longest at 6,650 km (though Amazon may actually be longer — disputed), flows north through Egypt to Mediterranean. Source: White Nile (Lake Victoria, Uganda) and Blue Nile (Ethiopia — brings 85% of water and silt). Annual flooding created the fertile black land (kemet) that enabled ancient Egyptian civilization. Yangtze (China, 6,300 km): longest in Asia. Three Gorges Dam. Congo (Africa): world's deepest river (~220m), second largest by volume, runs through one of Earth's few remaining large tropical rainforests. Mississippi-Missouri (USA, 6,275 km): drains 41% of the continental US. Rhine, Danube (Europe). Ganges (India): sacred to Hinduism. Mekong (Southeast Asia): vital to food security of 60+ million people.

Mountain ranges: Himalayas (Asia): formed by collision of Indian and Eurasian plates (~50 million years ago, still rising ~5mm/year). Contains 9 of the world's 10 highest peaks. Everest (8,848.86m), K2 (8,611m, second highest, more dangerous), Kangchenjunga (8,586m). Andes (South America): world's longest continental mountain range (~7,000 km), highest peak: Aconcagua (6,961m — highest outside Asia). Rich in copper, silver, gold. Rocky Mountains (North America): spine of the continent, Continental Divide — rivers flow either to Pacific or Atlantic. Alps (Europe): formed by African and Eurasian plate collision. Highest: Mont Blanc (4,808m). Atlas Mountains (Africa, Morocco/Algeria/Tunisia). Appalachians (eastern USA): ancient range, once as tall as Himalayas — 480 million years old, heavily eroded. Sierra Nevada (California): granite batholith. Volcanism: Cascades (Mt. Rainier, Mt. Hood, Mt. St. Helens). Mountain ecosystems: altitudinal zonation — different ecosystems at different elevations (foothills → montane forest → subalpine → alpine tundra → permanent snow/ice).

Deserts receive <250mm precipitation per year. Cover ~33% of Earth's land surface. Types: Hot desert (Sahara — 9.2 million km², world's largest hot desert; Sonoran; Arabian), Cold desert (Gobi, 1.3 million km², Asia; Patagonian; Taklamakan), Coastal desert (Atacama — driest non-polar desert on Earth, parts haven't had measurable rain in 500 years, despite being on the coast — cold Humboldt Current blocks moisture; also Namib), Polar desert (Antarctica — actually the world's largest desert at 14.2 million km², receives <200mm precipitation). Desert ecology: animals adapt via nocturnal behavior, burrowing, concentrated urine, water extraction from food. Camels: humps store fat (not water), can lose 25% body weight in water without harm, oval red blood cells continue flowing in dehydrated blood. Cacti (Americas): store water in succulent stems, CAM photosynthesis (open stomata only at night). Desert soils (aridisols): calcium carbonate hardpan, low organic matter, high pH. Desertification: degradation of drylands — ~12 million hectares/year affected.

Arctic vs Antarctic: Arctic (north): ocean surrounded by land (no continent) — Arctic Ocean covered by sea ice. Land around it: Alaska, Canada, Greenland, Scandinavia, Russia. Average winter temperature: −40°C, summer: 0°C. Antarctica (south): continent surrounded by ocean — covered by ice sheet up to 4.8km thick, contains 70% of Earth's fresh water. Average temperature: −57°C (lowest recorded: −89.2°C at Vostok Station). Ice loss: Arctic sea ice extent declining ~13%/decade (since 1979 satellite record). Greenland ice sheet losing ~280 billion tonnes/year. Antarctic ice sheet: East Antarctica mostly stable; West Antarctic Ice Sheet and Antarctic Peninsula destabilizing. If all Antarctic ice melted: sea levels would rise ~58m. Permafrost: permanently frozen ground covering ~24% of Northern Hemisphere land — stores ~1.7 trillion tonnes of organic carbon. Thawing permafrost releases methane (CH₄, 80× more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂ over 20 years) — a dangerous feedback loop. Arctic animals: polar bear, Arctic fox, narwhal, walrus, musk ox. Antarctic: penguins (NO polar bears — they exist only in the Arctic), seals, albatross, leopard seal.

Blockchain: a distributed ledger — a chain of blocks, each containing transactions and a cryptographic hash of the previous block (making tampering computationally infeasible). Decentralized: no central authority — thousands of nodes hold complete copies. Consensus mechanisms: Proof of Work (PoW): miners compete to solve cryptographic puzzles (SHA-256 for Bitcoin). Winner adds next block, earns reward. Energy intensive — Bitcoin uses ~127 TWh/year (~0.6% of global electricity). 51% attack: attacker controlling >51% of hash power could manipulate the chain.
