They get layers of ice as they cycle up and down, growing bigger each pass, until they're too heavy for the storm to hold up. Cut a hailstone open and you can see the rings, like a tiny onion.

Snow forms when water vapor high in cold clouds skips the liquid stage and freezes directly into ice crystals around tiny particles. The crystals grow into snowflakes as they fall through layers of cloud, with the exact temperature and humidity at each level shaping their delicate six-armed forms.

Rain forms when water droplets in clouds grow large enough to fall. Tiny droplets collide and merge as winds churn them around. When they're heavy enough that the updraft can't hold them, they fall. In cold clouds, ice crystals grow first, then melt as they drop through warmer air below.

Acid rain forms when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels mix with rain to make sulfuric and nitric acids. It damages forests, dissolves limestone statues, and acidifies lakes. Clean-air laws starting in the 1970s and 80s drastically reduced acid rain in North America and Europe — a real environmental success story.

Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere. The main ones are water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and ozone. CO2 is the biggest concern from human activity because we release so much of it and it sticks around for centuries. Methane is far more potent per molecule but breaks down within a couple of decades.

Fossil fuels — coal, oil, and natural gas — are the buried, compressed remains of plants and microorganisms from hundreds of millions of years ago. Burning them releases the carbon those ancient living things originally pulled from the air, in a fraction of the time. That's the heart of climate change.

Renewable energy comes from sources that naturally refill — sunlight, wind, water flow, geothermal heat, and biomass. Solar and wind have become cheaper than coal in many places. Combined with batteries and a smarter electrical grid, they're rapidly replacing fossil fuels in many countries — though decarbonizing transport, heat, and industry remains a major challenge.

Half-life is the time it takes for half of a radioactive sample to decay. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years, used for dating archaeological finds. Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.5 billion years. After 10 half-lives, only about 1/1000 of the original amount remains.

Carbon dating measures how much carbon-14 is left in old organic material. Living things keep refreshing their carbon-14 from the air; once they die, the supply stops decaying away. Comparing the amount left to the natural level tells you how long ago it died. The method is reliable out to about 50,000 years.

Fluorescent materials absorb high-energy light (often ultraviolet) and immediately re-emit it at a lower, visible energy. That's why white shirts can glow under black lights and why some minerals shine in eye-popping colors under UV. The trick is one of the cleanest ways to convert invisible light into visible light.

Phosphorescent materials, like glow-in-the-dark stickers, also absorb light and re-emit it — but they store the energy and let it out slowly over minutes or hours. The lag comes from electrons getting stuck in long-lived excited states. Charge them up with bright light and they'll glow softly long after the lights go out.

After the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, the most worrying releases were iodine-131 (half-life 8 days, gone within months) and cesium-137 (half-life 30 years, still around). Different isotopes call for very different responses — short-lived ones are intense but pass quickly; long-lived ones linger for generations.

Mars has a thin CO2 atmosphere and almost no greenhouse effect — surface temperatures average a chilly −60°C. Venus has a thick CO2 atmosphere and a runaway greenhouse effect that bakes its surface to 465°C, hot enough to melt lead. The same physics applies to Earth, which is why we worry about adding so much CO2 here.

A warming climate brings more intense heatwaves, rising seas, longer droughts in some regions and heavier rain in others, melting glaciers and Arctic ice, stronger hurricanes, and shifting habitats for plants and animals. Many effects feed back on each other, which is why scientists urge cutting greenhouse emissions sooner rather than later.

Multiple independent lines of evidence point to human-caused warming: rising temperatures match the timing and amount of CO2 from fossil fuels; the carbon isotope mix matches fossil sources; nights are warming faster than days (a fingerprint of greenhouse warming, not the Sun); and the stratosphere is cooling (incompatible with solar heating). Studies show over 97% of climate scientists agree.

Scientists warn we're in the middle of a sixth mass extinction, this one driven by human activity — habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and overharvesting. Species are dying off at rates hundreds to thousands of times higher than the long-term background rate. Unlike previous extinctions, this one has a known cause we could in principle slow or reverse.
